name: liburing_b3sum
baseline: official Rust b3sum (read/mmap based) and cat to /dev/null
workload: Cold-cache BLAKE3 hash of a 1 GiB and a 10 GiB file on NVMe using an io_uring ring-buffer reader (O_DIRECT, queue depth 2-4, 512 KiB blocks).
claimed_speedup: 1 GiB cold: 0.301s vs 0.381s (b3sum --no-mmap) and 0.404-0.416s (b3sum 1 thread); 10 GiB: 2.899s vs cat to /dev/null 2.904s; author says ~25% faster than official b3sum and at NVMe line rate
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 -D_GNU_SOURCE ... -luring libblake3.a (GCC 11.2.0 for the b3sum example); Debian 12, kernel 6.1.0-9, ext4
hardware: NVMe drive advertised at 3500MB/s; CPU model not stated (author mentions AMD64 with sha_ni and AVX2, no AVX512)
tradeoffs: Single-threaded variant needs O_DIRECT to be fast; hashing only, a demo program rather than a library; depends on liburing and libblake3.
caveats: First-party blog numbers, CPU model not stated so tier C. No license file (LICENSE returned 404), so reference only. Gain over cat is within noise; the real gap is versus Rust b3sum on a cold disk. Page cache flushed before each run, so it is I/O-bound by design.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'fast file hashing sync tool io_uring C benchmark faster than sha256sum b3sum' (BLAKE3 issue #328 led to the repo)

name: bfs
workload: Full traversal of a home directory of about 7.6 million files with -false (directory walk only), warm cache.
claimed_speedup: bfs 3.0.1 ran 2.91 +/- 0.03 times faster than find and 3.40 +/- 0.03 times faster than fd, and 2.20x faster than bfs 2.6.3 (from the search snippet of the author's blog post)
tradeoffs: Breadth-first order differs from find's depth-first order; mostly find-compatible but not identical; uses queued/threaded getdents-style I/O.
caveats: Numbers come from the blocked blog post; read from a WebSearch snippet only (snippet only). Blog is first-party and from 2023, so later find/fd versions may differ. Repo README makes no numeric claim. This is a directory-walk tool rather than an I/O library.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'fast directory traversal benchmark getdents64 vs readdir vs fts library faster than find'

name: fclones
baseline: jdupes / fdupes / rdfind (duplicate finders built on POSIX read)
workload: Find duplicates among 1,460,720 paths (316 GB) on NVMe SSD, page cache dropped before each run; second HDD benchmark of 51,370 paths.
claimed_speedup: SSD: fclones 0:34.59 vs rmlint 2:28.43, jdupes 5:01.91, fdupes 5:46.19, rdfind 5:53.07, yadf 0:59.32
hardware: Dell Precision 5520, Intel Xeon E3-1505M v6 3.00GHz, 32GB RAM, 512GB NVMe, Ubuntu 20.10 kernel 5.8.0-53
tradeoffs: Rust, not directly callable from C++; end-user tool; parallel scan and physical-offset ordering for HDD.
caveats: First-party benchmark with no script or dataset published, so tier C. Version numbers date from 2021 (fclones 0.12.1). Baseline is other duplicate finders, not raw POSIX read. Not a C++ library.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'fclones benchmark duplicate file finder fdupes jdupes rdfind rmlint comparison times'

name: fcp
workload: Copy the Linux kernel source tree and a directory of 13 x 512 MB files; parallel directory walk and copy.
claimed_speedup: Linux (XFS, a1.metal): kernel tree 675 ms vs 6.02 s (~10x), large files 8 s vs 11.3 s (~1.4x); macOS APFS: kernel tree 5.1 s vs 30 s (~6x), large files ~822x (copy-on-write clones)
hardware: AWS EC2 a1.metal (16 CPUs, 32 GiB RAM, SSD, XFS); 2018 MacBook Pro 2.9 GHz 6-core i9 APFS
tradeoffs: Rust CLI; does not cover cp's many options; poor on HDDs; Unix only.
caveats: Results are bar charts embedded as images with averages in alt text; benchmark script not seen. The macOS 822x figure is clonefile copy-on-write rather than faster data movement. Not a C++ library.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'Rust fast file copy fcp benchmark cp rsync parallel faster than cp'

name: parallel-disk-usage (pdu)
workload: Disk usage scan of a large directory tree, warm cache, with and without hardlink deduplication; benchmark produced by a GitHub Actions workflow.
claimed_speedup: Reported in search snippets as pdu 299.1 ms vs dust 578.7 ms, du 1255.2 ms, ncdu 2222.4 ms on a 90 GB tree with 100k dirs and 400k files (snippet only, README itself gives charts); another run pdu 0.24.0 median 1.061 s vs dust 1.754 s, ncdu 3.004 s
hardware: GitHub Actions runners (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Rust CLI/library crate, not callable from C++ directly; output is a chart tree.
caveats: Public workflow and published raw data in separate benchmark repos, but CPU model is not stated and the figures I quoted are from snippets or SVG charts; tier B at most. Competitor 'du' is a single-threaded walk, so the gain is parallelism.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'parallel-disk-usage pdu benchmark faster than du dust ncdu hyperfine'

name: InstantTensor
baseline: safetensors loader (mmap-based file read to GPU); also compared with fastsafetensors and Run:ai Model Streamer
workload: Load Qwen3-30B-A3B (61 GB) on 1 H200 and DeepSeek-R1 (689 GB) on 8 H200 from 50 GB/s storage using direct I/O with tuned io_uring/AIO concurrency; also tmpfs.
claimed_speedup: 50GB/s storage: Qwen3-30B-A3B 1.77 s vs safetensors 57.4 s (32.4x), fastsafetensors 22.2 s, RMS 9.29 s; DeepSeek-R1 15.3 s vs 160 s (10.5x). tmpfs: 1.26 s vs 12.7 s (10.1x) and 12.1 s vs 22.6 s (1.87x)
hardware: H200 GPUs, 50 GB/s storage; tmpfs testbed 2 NUMA nodes x 8 channels DDR5; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: C++ core with Python API aimed at PyTorch/GPU loading; direct I/O makes warm-cache loads slower than page-cache-based loaders; needs very fast storage to show the gain.
caveats: First-party benchmark; CPU model, compiler flags and the loader scripts are not given, so tier C. Baseline is safetensors via Python, not a raw POSIX read loop. A repo (123123213weqw/siphon) republishes the identical table and is not reported separately.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'fast model weights loader io_uring O_DIRECT C++ safetensors mmap comparison load time benchmark'

name: Run:ai Model Streamer
baseline: Hugging Face safetensors loader (mmap/read) and Tensorizer
workload: Load Meta-Llama-3-8B (15 GB, single safetensors file) to one A10G GPU from cold start on AWS GP3 SSD, IO2 SSD and S3 with concurrent reads.
claimed_speedup: GP3 SSD: 14.34 s at concurrency 16 vs 47.99 s for the safetensors loader (3.3x, derived from page data); concurrency 1 matches safetensors at 47.56 s. InstantTensor's table (50GB/s storage) shows RMS 9.29 s vs safetensors 57.4 s (6.18x)
hardware: AWS g5.12xlarge (4x A10G, one used); GP3 750 GB 1000 MiB/s, IO2 500 GB 4000 MiB/s
tradeoffs: C++ core with Python bindings; concurrency parameter must be tuned; also reads from S3.
caveats: First-party benchmark from 2024 versions (Model Streamer 0.6.0, vLLM 0.5.5), CPU model and flags not stated. The GP3 result hit the volume's 1 GiB/s cap, so it measures concurrency against a throttled disk. Tier C.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): InstantTensor benchmark table (docs/benchmark.md) listing RMS as a competitor

name: fastsafetensors
workload: Load GPT-2 and larger models on AMD MI300X (ROCm, no GDS) with parallel threads and fixed buffers versus mmap; paper also reports Llama/Falcon/Bloom loads.
claimed_speedup: ROCm nogds: 6.02 GB/s vs mmap 1.28 GB/s (4.7x) for GPT-2 Medium; 2.62 GB/s vs 1.01 GB/s (2.6x) for GPT-2; README: 4.8x-7.5x faster than default safetensors, 26.4 GB/s on Llama-70B with GDS
tradeoffs: Python library with native extension (not usable from C++ directly); avoids mmap and the page cache; advantage vanishes when the model is already cached (InstantTensor's table shows 0.76x vs safetensors on tmpfs).
caveats: Peer-reviewed CLOUD 2025 paper (arXiv 2505.23072) was not opened (arXiv blocked), so only the repo's own report was used; tier C. Numbers in the ROCm report come from a small model and CPU model is not stated.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'fast model weights loader io_uring O_DIRECT C++ safetensors mmap comparison load time benchmark'

name: ptar
workload: Archive the Linux kernel source (1.5 GB, 47K files) and a 10 TB, 500K-file dataset on GPFS with hot page pool, no compression, N parallel workers writing separate valid tar files.
claimed_speedup: Kernel tree: gnutar 6m4s vs 64 workers 9.4 s (~38x, derived from page data); 10TB set: gnutar 10hr20m vs 32 workers 44m39s
hardware: GPFS with hot page pool (no CPU model)
tradeoffs: Produces N independent tar files rather than one archive; Go tool, not callable from C++.
caveats: First-party numbers on a parallel file system with hot cache; 1 worker is slower than GNU tar (6m33s); no flags or versions given.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'tar archive extraction fast parallel C++ benchmark faster than GNU tar bsdtar libarchive io_uring'

name: zdu
baseline: dust and pdu (disk usage tools built on parallel stat/readdir)
workload: Disk usage scan of ~/.cargo (57k files), ~/programs (509k files) and /nix/store (1.2M files), hyperfine, warm page cache, 32 logical cores.
claimed_speedup: 509k files: 143.8 ms vs dust 388.2 ms (2.7x) and pdu -H 228.3 ms (1.6x); 1.2M files: 402.7 ms vs dust 1.118 s and pdu 1.401 s (3.5x); 57k files: 19.6 ms vs pdu 14.0 ms (1.40x slower)
tradeoffs: Rust CLI; not a C++ library; baselines are other fast tools, not du.
caveats: Brand-new, first-party, warm cache only; loses to pdu on the smallest tree. Included as a shootout winner against dust and pdu.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'parallel-disk-usage pdu benchmark faster than du dust ncdu github hyperfine'
